title: The Anthropic Economic Index — interactive hub for understanding AI's effects on the economy
author: Anthropic

dom.t: Observed use: Capability predictions exceed workplace adoption

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source provides only a descriptive occupational usage snapshot, including lawyers’ 0.62% share and higher usage in several computing roles. It offers no task-level capability evidence, causal analysis, or findings on expertise, verification, selective deployment, or operating-model redesign, so its position on the cluster’s proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Exposure rankings: Different measures reorder legal work
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by reporting occupational AI usage rather than computerisation probabilities or observed displacement. Its figures place lawyers at 0.62% and show different usage levels across diverse occupations, but provide no basis for staffing or employment-loss conclusions.

st.t: Observed use: Capability predictions exceed workplace adoption
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s task-level framing by distinguishing automation, collaboration and human-led work, and by explicitly warning that observed conversation categories are not users’ occupations. It provides descriptive adoption evidence rather than independently establishing the claimed gap between predicted capability and workplace adoption.

kp.d: The dashboard defines its geographic usage index as observed Claude use relative to use expected from population: values above 1 indicate greater-than-expected use and values below 1 indicate less-than-expected use. The displayed data concern Claude.ai conversations, not total use of all AI systems.
qs: Understand if a state uses Claude more (>1) or less (<1) than expected, based on its population.
Understand if a country uses Claude more (>1) or less (<1) than expected, based on its population.
The world map shows data on Claude.ai conversations.

kp.k: Claude usage varies substantially across US jurisdictions
kp.d: In the displayed US ranking, Washington, D.C. has the highest per-capita usage index at 3.32, followed by California at 1.62, New York at 1.55, Washington at 1.51 and Massachusetts at 1.42. The dashboard ranks 51 jurisdictions, including D.C.; this is a comparative usage finding rather than evidence about economic or employment effects.

kp.k: International usage is also geographically unequal
kp.d: The country view ranks Australia first among 121 listed countries, with a usage index of 6.40 relative to an expected value of 1. Singapore, Switzerland, Luxembourg and New Zealand follow in the displayed ranking. These figures measure population-adjusted Claude.ai usage, not workforce exposure, productivity or displacement.
qs: - Australia  1  - Singapore  2  - Switzerland  3  - Luxembourg  4  - New Zealand  5

kp.k: Computer-related tasks form the largest usage category
kp.d: When conversations are grouped through O*NET-SOC task classifications, computer and mathematical activities account for 21.7% of displayed usage. Arts, design, entertainment, sports and media account for 14.5%; educational instruction and library activities for 13.4%; sales for 8.9%; and office and administrative support for 8.4%.
qs: Arts, Design, Entertainment, Sports, and Media  14.5%

kp.k: Task classifications do not identify users’ occupations
kp.d: Anthropic expressly qualifies the occupational presentation: percentages describe conversations associated with tasks or task groups, rather than the job titles of the people using Claude. Privacy filtering also prevents the displayed percentages from summing to 100%, limiting comprehensive interpretation of the distribution.
qs: Percentages represent the share of Claude.ai conversations associated with each task or group of tasks.

kp.k: Automation and augmentation differ by task
kp.d: The dashboard presents automation and augmentation as task-dependent collaboration patterns rather than uniform properties of an occupation. It states that people delegate some task components, such as data entry, while using Claude collaboratively for exploration and problem-solving; other tasks do not appear in the usage data and remain human-performed.
qs: See how people prefer to work with Claude—collaborating together or fully delegating tasks.

kp.d: Among the displayed O*NET-derived job groupings, Document Management Specialists have the largest usage share at 5.10%, followed by Librarians and Media Collections Specialists at 4.22%, Counter and Rental Clerks at 2.72%, Editors at 2.58% and Writers and Authors at 2.22%. Because the dashboard groups task data into job titles, these shares should not be read as percentages of workers in those occupations using Claude.

kp.d: The occupation-grouped display assigns 0.62% of Claude.ai conversation usage to the Lawyers grouping within the Legal category. The excerpt provides no further breakdown of legal tasks, users, firm roles, automation levels, pricing effects or professional-rule implications, and its task-versus-job caveat applies to this figure.

kp.k: Local topic mixes illustrate differing use cases
kp.d: The dashboard reports different common conversational topics by geography. In Washington, D.C., self-presentation writing and homework are the two largest listed topics, while homework leads in Australia, followed by business operations, self-presentation writing, promotional writing and workplace writing. These are descriptive conversation shares, not measures of task success or economic impact.

kp.k: Dashboard distinguishes work, personal and coursework use
kp.d: The index separates Claude.ai conversations into work, personal and coursework contexts rather than treating all usage as occupational. This distinction qualifies any inference from overall conversation shares to labour-market adoption, because some observed use is explicitly non-work or educational.
qs: See how Claude usage breaks down across work, personal, and coursework contexts.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Anthropic describes task-level automation and augmentation, rather than predicting wholesale replacement of occupations.
pts.d: The Economic Index states that people delegate some job tasks, such as data entry, while using Claude collaboratively to explore problems or ideas. It also states that other tasks remain in human hands. This is a cross-domain description of current usage, not a forecast of employment losses or a legal-services-specific prediction.

pts.k: Anthropic reports uneven usage across task categories, including a 0.62% conversation share associated with lawyer tasks.
pts.d: The dashboard associates 21.7% of Claude.ai conversations with Computer and Mathematical tasks, 14.5% with Arts, Design, Entertainment, Sports, and Media, and 13.4% with Educational Instruction and Library. The Lawyers entry reports 0.62% usage. These are shares of conversations associated with occupational tasks, not the percentage of lawyers using AI, the share of legal work automated, or the occupational identities of users. The captured source makes no further concrete claim about changes in legal services.

pts.k: Anthropic reports geographic differences in Claude usage relative to population.
pts.d: The dashboard defines its Usage Index relative to population-based expected usage. Washington, D.C. ranks first among 51 U.S. jurisdictions at 3.32 times expected usage; Australia ranks first among 121 country-level entries at 6.40 times expected usage. These are descriptive adoption-pattern claims, not estimates of productivity or economic impact.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is Anthropic's Claude.ai conversation data, organised into task, occupational, geographic, and collaboration categories.
pts.d: Anthropic groups tasks using O*NET-SOC classifications and reports conversation shares and population-normalised usage indices. It distinguishes automation from augmentation through collaboration categories. The captured text does not provide a sample size, collection window, detailed classification-validation procedure, or causal evidence about employment and productivity. Although the interface lists metrics such as task success and human-with-AI time, it supplies no corresponding results supporting claims of time savings or performance improvements.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source presents a current-usage snapshot last updated June 26, 2026, with explicit coverage and privacy qualifications and no forecast horizon.
pts.d: The supplied dashboard capture is dated July 27, 2026, while the page states that it was last updated June 26, 2026. Its underlying observation period is not specified. Findings concern Claude.ai conversations rather than AI use economy-wide. Privacy filters mean reported task shares do not sum to 100%. Geographic coverage also depends on service availability. The dashboard category 'Tasks that don't appear in our data' describes absence from the dataset, not proof that such tasks cannot be automated.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source concerns people using Claude across occupational tasks and work, personal, and coursework contexts; it does not identify legal-market consequences.
pts.d: The reported task categories span computing, creative work, education, sales, administration, science, and legal work, among others. Users may delegate tasks or collaborate with Claude, with patterns varying geographically. Lawyer-associated tasks appear in the dashboard, but the source does not distinguish law firms, in-house departments, clients, or alternative legal service providers, and offers no claims about legal fees, staffing, hiring, or access to justice. Occupational task labels must not be treated as identification of users' actual jobs.
